items.title: 0.9999... equals 1, exactly
items.claim: The decimal expansion 0.999... (infinitely many 9s) does not approach 1 — it IS 1. Two different decimal expansions can represent the same real number.

options.text: They're approximately equal but slightly different
They have zero difference (1 - 0.999... = 0); 0.999... = sum of 9/10 to the n for n from 1 to infinity = 9/10 / (1 - 1/10) = 1 exactly

items.reveal:
Every infinite decimal expansion is, by definition, a convergent series.
0.999... = 9/10 + 9/100 + 9/1000 + ...
     = 9/10 * (1 + 1/10 + 1/100 + ...)
     = 9/10 * 1/(1 - 1/10)
     = 9/10 * 10/9
     = 1

Another argument: let x = 0.999... Then 10x = 9.999... Subtract: 10x - x = 9.999... - 0.999... so 9x = 9 and x = 1.

Third argument: the difference 1 - 0.999... is less than 10 to the minus n for every n. The only non-negative real with this property is 0. So 1 - 0.999... = 0 and 0.999... = 1.

Decimals are a representation, not an identity. Any real with a terminating decimal also has a 999...-style alternative: 0.5 = 0.4999..., 1 = 0.999..., 0.123 = 0.122999... The two representations are equal.

In educational settings this is one of the most strongly contested results — students often refuse to accept it. The objection is usually based on confusing representations with the numbers themselves.
items.why: Decimals feel like unique addresses for numbers. They are not — every terminating decimal has a recurring-9 twin, and equality of the two is logically forced.

items.title: 1 is the first digit of natural numbers 30% of the time
items.claim: Take any 'natural' set of numbers — house prices, river lengths, populations, physical constants. Look at the first digit. About 30% start with 1. Only 4.6% start with 9. The pattern is so reliable that auditors use it to detect fraud.

options.text: Benford's law: for scale-invariant distributions, the probability of first digit d is log10(1 + 1/d). The math reflects that doubling a number (or scaling by any factor) takes longer to pass through 1-2 than through 8-9 on a logarithmic axis

items.reveal:
Simon Newcomb (1881) noticed that the early pages of his logarithm tables (corresponding to leading digit 1) were more worn than the later pages. He inferred something about how often various leading digits appeared.

Frank Benford (1938, physicist) systematically tested the rule across many datasets (river lengths, populations, atomic weights, baseball stats, addresses). He found:
Digit 1: 30.1%
Digit 2: 17.6%
Digit 3: 12.5%
Digit 4: 9.7%
Digit 5: 7.9%
Digit 6: 6.7%
Digit 7: 5.8%
Digit 8: 5.1%
Digit 9: 4.6%
Formula: P(d) = log10(1 + 1/d).

Why: many natural quantities span multiple orders of magnitude. On a logarithmic scale, the spacing from 1 to 2 (log 2 ≈ 0.30) is much wider than from 9 to 10 (log 10/9 ≈ 0.046). If the distribution is roughly uniform in log space, leading digits follow Benford.

Applications:
- Forensic accounting: real financial data follow Benford; fabricated numbers usually don't. Auditors flag tax returns or financial statements that deviate.
- Election fraud detection: ballot counts in honest elections follow Benford; many disputed elections have shown deviations.
- Scientific fraud detection: many cases of data fabrication caught.
- Image authenticity: pixel JPEG coefficients follow Benford-like distributions; fakes often don't.

Limitations: Benford requires scale-invariant data spanning multiple orders of magnitude. Constrained data (height, ages) don't satisfy it. Carefully fabricated data designed to fool Benford also exist.

The mathematical generalisation: any distribution with logarithmic density invariant under scaling will produce Benford's law for leading digits.
items.why: Random-looking data often follow precise patterns. Benford's law is counterintuitive and has practical applications in fraud detection. It's also a window into how scale-invariance shapes the structure of numbers we encounter.

items.title: A game with infinite expected payoff that no one will pay $20 to play
items.claim: Flip a fair coin. If heads, you win 2 dollars. If tails, you flip again — heads pays 4, etc. After n tails, the next heads pays 2 to the n+1 dollars. The expected payoff is infinite. People offered the game won't pay more than 10 to 20 dollars to play.
items.prompt: Why doesn't expected value match human behaviour?

options.text: Humans value money non-linearly — losing 100 dollars hurts more than the equivalent fraction of utility of gaining 100; Bernoulli proposed logarithmic utility, giving a finite expected utility despite infinite expected dollars
The game is impossible to play

items.reveal:
The expected value: (1/2)(2) + (1/4)(4) + (1/8)(8) + ... = 1 + 1 + 1 + ... = infinity. So by pure expected-value reasoning, any finite price for the game is a great deal.

Daniel Bernoulli (1738) noted that no rational person actually pays a large sum to play. He proposed that humans value money according to a logarithmic utility function, not linearly. Expected utility for the game with log utility is finite (about ln 2 plus a small constant), giving a reasonable price.

The St. Petersburg paradox launched expected utility theory (von Neumann, Morgenstern, 1944), behavioural economics (Kahneman, Tversky, 1979), and theories of risk aversion. It's one of the founding puzzles of decision theory.

It also exposes a deeper issue: the game has finite real-world payoff (the casino can't pay infinite money), so a more accurate model bounds the prize, giving a finite expected value of perhaps 20 dollars — close to what people actually pay.
items.why: Expected value is treated as the rational basis for decision-making. The St. Petersburg paradox shows it can be unbounded for games with bounded reasonable price — and that human utility is non-linear.
